title: Those who saw and overlooked
hookLine: those who saw others' faults and chose to overlook them

cards: Your roommate leaves the dishes again. A coworker takes credit for something you did. Your brother says the thing he always says at family dinners.
You see it. You absolutely see it. And then there's a fork in the road, a split second where you decide what to do with what you saw.

The path there is well worn: file it away, bring it up later, tell someone else. The Ardas, in its list of people Sikhs remember with honor, includes one group whose only deed is what they did at that fork.

teach.b: Right after those who shared their food, ran the kitchen and wielded the sword, the Ardas adds: dekh ke andith keetaa. Dekh ke: having seen. Andith: unseen.

teach.h: ANDITH KEETAA: THEY MADE IT UNSEEN.
teach.b: Having seen, they made it unseen. It doesn't say they didn't notice. They weren't naive.
They saw clearly, and then chose to treat it as if they hadn't. Sikhs hear it first about other people's faults and the wrongs done to them: they saw, and let it go.
Some also hear it about temptation: they saw what could have pulled them off course, and looked away. Gurbani has the same spirit elsewhere.

teach.h: FARID: DO GOOD TO THE ONE WHO HARMS.
teach.b: Among the saloks of Sheikh Farid, the Sufi saint whose verses are in the Guru Granth Sahib, one says, in paraphrase: do good even to the one who does you harm, and don't let anger settle in your mind. Now, a balance.
The very same line honors those who wielded the sword. So overlooking isn't pretending injustice doesn't exist, or refusing to protect people. A Sikh is asked to stand up against cruelty.
Andith is about something smaller and more daily: the slights, the irritations, the faults of the people around you that you could keep score of, and don't.
A family, a friendship, a shared kitchen: each runs partly on people who quietly decided not to mention it. The Ardas puts them on the same list as the steadfast. Their deed was invisible on purpose.

how: In every Ardas Sikhs remember those who saw others' faults and overlooked them, dekh ke andith keetaa, alongside the steadfast and those who shared, served and protected.

o: hidden away so that no one else can find it
not noticed at all, missed through carelessness
unseen: seen clearly, then chosen not to hold

games.q: those who saw and overlooked — tap the pairs.
p: do good to the one who harms you

s: dekh ke andith keetaa describes people who didn't notice
they saw clearly, then chose to treat it as unseen.
the same Ardas line also honors those who wielded the sword
Sheikh Farid's verses are in the Guru Granth Sahib
one salok says do good even to the one who harms you.

games.q: your coworker takes credit for something small you did. you see it. by dekh ke andith keetaa, what do the people in the Ardas do?
o: see it, and let it go.
games.why: they saw, and made it unseen. the Ardas puts them on the same list as the steadfast and the sharers.

practice: Let one small irritation come to mind, something someone does that you keep noticing; not a real wrong that needs facing, just something small.
See it clearly, once, then picture yourself setting it down, the way you'd put a pebble from your shoe back on the path. If you pray, say Waheguru as you set it down.

wordCard.voice: Andith, unseen. Dekh ke andith keetaa: having seen clearly, they chose to make it unseen.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: andith, unseen; dekh ke andith keetaa, having seen, they made it unseen.

carryVoice: Your line: see, and overlook. Seeing clearly comes first, and letting go comes second. Day six hundred twenty-three, done.
